title: The Tree That Eats Air
blurb: A tree builds its whole body out of air, water, and sunlight, and keeps a diary of every year it lived inside its own wood.

blocks.text: A tree has three big parts. The roots are under the ground. They hold the tree down and drink water from the soil. The trunk is the tall part in the middle. 3.title: The Tree That Eats Air
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: One ring equals one year

blocks.prompt: The Diary Inside the Wood
blocks.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you find circles inside, one inside the next, like a target. Those circles are called rings, and they are a record. Each ring is one year of the tree's life. Here is why they form. In spring, when there is plenty of water, the tree grows fast and makes wide, pale wood. Later in the year it slows down and makes narrow, dark wood. One pale band plus one dark band equals one year. Count the dark bands and you know how old the tree is. The rings say more than that. A fat ring means a good year, with rain and sun and easy growing. A thin ring means a hard one, maybe a year with no rain. A black curved scar means a fire came through and the tree lived. Scientists read tree rings the way you would read a diary. A tree that lived four thousand years holds four thousand years of weather in its wood, written down while it happened, and it never once got the date wrong. The oldest known single tree is a bristlecone pine in California named Methuselah. It is about four thousand eight hundred years old. It was already growing when the pyramids were built.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.

What does a thin ring tell you about that year?
Why do you think a tree ring is a better record of old weather than a person's memory?
answers: one year of the tree's life
there is plenty of water, so the tree grows fast
it was a hard year, maybe a year with no rain
(inference: the tree wrote it down while it happened and cannot forget or get the date wrong)

4.title: The Tree That Eats Air
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Dry wood is about half carbon
That carbon came out of the air
Leaves build sugar from air, water, and light
Van Helmont weighed a willow for five years
Trees give off the oxygen we breathe

blocks.prompt: Knocking on Old Air
blocks.text: Here is a question that sounds silly until you try to answer it. A tree seed weighs less than a paperclip. A grown oak weighs many tons. Where did all that extra stuff come from? Almost everyone guesses the soil. It is the obvious answer. The tree is standing in dirt, its roots are buried in dirt, so the tree must be eating dirt. About four hundred years ago a scientist named Jan Baptist van Helmont decided to check. He put exactly two hundred pounds of dried soil in a pot, planted a small willow in it, and gave it nothing but water for five years. Then he weighed everything again. The willow had gained more than one hundred and sixty pounds. The soil had lost about two ounces. The dirt was still there. So the tree was not made of dirt. Here is what actually happens. Leaves have tiny holes in them that let air in. Air contains carbon dioxide, a gas made of carbon and oxygen. Inside the leaf, sunlight provides the energy to break that gas apart and join the carbon to water pulled up from the roots. The result is sugar. The tree builds that sugar into wood, and it throws the leftover oxygen away into the air, which is lucky for us, because we breathe it. Dry wood is about half carbon by weight, and every one of those carbon atoms floated in as a gas. So when you knock on a tree trunk, you are knocking on old air. The tree caught it, one molecule at a time, and made it solid.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.

Where does the carbon in a tree trunk come from, and how does it get there?
The passage says the leftover oxygen is lucky for us. Why?
answers: (he was testing whether the tree ate soil; the soil barely changed while the willow gained over 160 pounds)
(inference: the tree gained far more weight than the soil lost, so the mass could not have come from the dirt)
from carbon dioxide gas in the air, taken in through tiny holes in the leaves
(we breathe the oxygen trees release as waste)

answers: A tree builds most of its body out of a gas it pulls from the air, not out of soil

5.title: The Tree That Eats Air
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Hyperion, a coast redwood, is about 380 feet tall
There is no pump anywhere in a tree
Water is pulled up, not pushed
A suction straw quits at about 33 feet
Xylem: the pipes running root to leaf
A big oak can move 100 gallons in a day

blocks.prompt: The Rope of Water
blocks.text: Hyperion is a coast redwood in northern California. It stands about 380 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty. Every day, water leaves the soil at Hyperion's roots and arrives in leaves nearly forty stories up. There is no pump anywhere in the tree. There is no heart, no muscle, nothing that squeezes. So how does the water get up there? Start with what should be impossible. If you drop a straw down a well and suck on the top, you cannot lift water higher than about thirty-three feet. It does not matter how hard you suck or how good your pump is. Above thirty-three feet the weight of the water column beats the air pressure pushing it up, and the water simply stops. By that rule, no tree should be taller than a three-story building. Trees do not suck. They pull, and the difference matters. Inside the trunk are xylem vessels, narrow pipes running from root to leaf, each one filled with an unbroken thread of water. Water molecules cling to one another. They are sticky in a way most liquids are not, because each molecule tugs weakly on its neighbors. So the water in a xylem vessel behaves less like a liquid and more like a rope. Now go up to a leaf on a warm afternoon. The leaf has tiny pores in it, and water evaporates out through them into the air. Every molecule that escapes tugs on the one behind it, and that one tugs on the next, and the pull travels all the way down the rope to the roots. Nobody pushes. The whole column is dragged upward by evaporation happening in the leaves, a few molecules at a time, all day long. A big oak can move a hundred gallons of water this way between sunrise and sunset. The water inside a tall tree is therefore under tension. It is stretched. Pull hard enough and the thread snaps, an air bubble forms, and that pipe stops working for good. This is the tree's real ceiling. In 2004, researchers who climbed the tallest redwoods to measure them calculated that gravity and friction together should stop any tree at somewhere around 400 to 430 feet. Hyperion is at 380. It is already near the edge of what physics allows.

6.title: The Tree That Eats Air
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Mycorrhiza: a root and fungus partnership
About nine in ten land plants use it
The deal is over 400 million years old
Simard tracked carbon moving tree to tree in 1997
Nature nicknamed it the wood wide web
In 2023 three scientists found the story overstated

blocks.prompt: The Wood Wide Web, and What We Actually Know
blocks.text: Walk into a forest and you see trees standing apart from one another, each one quiet, each one alone. Almost everything interesting about that scene is happening where you cannot see it. Under your feet, the soil is threaded with fungi. Not mushrooms, exactly. A mushroom is only the fruit. The body of the fungus is a web of filaments called hyphae, thinner than a human hair, running through the dirt in every direction. Roughly nine out of ten plant species on land partner with these fungi. The fungus wraps around or grows into a tree's roots and makes a trade. The tree hands over sugar it built from sunlight. The fungus hands back water and minerals like phosphorus, which its thin threads can reach in pockets of soil too small for a root to enter. Both sides do better than they would alone. This partnership is called mycorrhiza, and it is one of the oldest deals in biology, older than trees themselves. Then, in 1997, a forest ecologist named Suzanne Simard published a result that changed how people talk about forests. She fed Douglas fir and paper birch trees carbon dioxide made from unusual carbon atoms she could track. Later, she found the tracked carbon inside trees she had never fed. It had moved underground, tree to tree, through fungi. A commentary in the journal Nature gave the idea a name that stuck: the wood wide web. The nickname did a lot of work, and not all of it good. Within twenty years the story had grown into something else. Forests were described as networks where mother trees recognized their own seedlings and deliberately fed them, where trees warned each other about insect attacks, where the whole forest behaved like a single cooperative mind. It is a lovely story. It appeared in bestsellers, documentaries, and school assemblies. In 2023, three scientists sat down and checked it. Justine Karst, Melanie Jones, and Jason Hoeksema went back through the published research and asked a simple question: does the evidence support what people are saying? Their answer, in short, was no. They found that the strongest claims rested on very few field studies, that papers citing those studies routinely overstated what the studies had found, and that the overstatements got repeated until they sounded like settled fact. Some claims had never been tested in a mature forest at all. Notice what they did not say. They did not say the fungi are imaginary. Mycorrhizal partnerships are real, measured, and essential. Carbon really does move between trees underground. What they said is narrower and more useful: we do not yet know how much of it happens in real forests, whether trees choose where it goes, or whether the seedling on the receiving end is helped, ignored, or quietly farmed by a fungus running its own business. That last possibility is worth sitting with. Nothing about the trade requires kindness. A fungus connected to two trees is not a telephone line between friends. It is an organism with its own interests, moving resources in whatever direction serves the fungus. The generous forest and the self-interested fungus produce the same data. Telling them apart takes work that has mostly not been done yet. So the honest version is less comforting and more interesting than the one you have probably heard. Underneath the forest floor there is a vast, ancient, living network that we can measure but cannot yet read. We know the trades happen. We do not know who is deciding. Science is allowed to end there, and it is allowed to stay there until somebody does the experiment.
